title: "Nucleus Sampling (Top-p)"
description: "A text-generation decoding method that samples from the smallest set of likely next tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p."
term: "Nucleus Sampling (Top-p)"
letter: "N"
category: "LLM Engineering"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Nucleus sampling, or top-p sampling, lets a language model choose its next
token from a dynamically sized group of likely options. It includes the
most probable tokens until their probabilities add up to at least a chosen
value $p$.

## Technical explanation

Given next-token probabilities sorted from largest to smallest,
top-p selects the smallest prefix whose cumulative probability is at least
$p$, then samples from that restricted distribution after renormalizing
the probabilities.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Top-p is a decoding control that can balance predictable and varied text.
Its behavior depends on the model distribution and interacts with
temperature and other decoding settings; it does not change model weights
or guarantee factual output.

## How it works

For token probabilities $p_1 \ge p_2 \ge \cdots$, find the smallest $k$
such that $\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i \ge p$. The sampler retains those $k$ tokens,
renormalizes their probabilities to sum to one, and samples one token.
The candidate set can vary from step to step.

## Practical example

If a prompt yields token probabilities $0.50$, $0.30$, $0.15$, and $0.05$,
with $p=0.8$, the first two tokens form the nucleus. The generated token
is sampled from those two after their probabilities are renormalized.

## Common misconceptions

- Top-p is not the same as top-k: top-p chooses a probability-mass threshold, while top-k fixes the number of candidates.
- A higher $p$ generally admits more candidate tokens but does not guarantee better writing.
- Sampling settings affect variation, not the underlying truth or reliability of the model's knowledge.
